title: What a hadith is
hook: a report of what the Prophet ﷺ said, did, or approved

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the pillars with the weakest pillar, and your line: strengthen one. Did you take your small step, even once? Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

Someone once asked Aisha a plain, domestic question: what did the Prophet do at home? Not in the mosque, not on the battlefield. At home. Her answer is preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari. He was busy serving his family, she said, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. That small answer has been carried, person to person and then book to book, so that it can be heard today. It's a report. And a new block of this year begins with that kind of report: what it is, how it travels, and how it's tested. Today, the hadith.
screen: `WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?` → `AISHA ANSWERS.` → `A REPORT, CARRIED.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word hadith is usually put into English as a report, or news. In Islamic scholarship it names a report about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and scholars sort those reports by what they carry. First, what he said. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe. One sentence, a whole ethic, in his own words as remembered. Second, what he did. That's Aisha's answer from the hook: no command at all, only a description. Serving his family, then rising for prayer. A deed reported becomes a teaching, because the people around him watched how he lived. Third, what he approved, the easiest one to miss. Also in Bukhari: a companion who led prayers kept ending his recitation with one short surah, al-Ikhlas. When the people came back, they mentioned it to the Prophet. He didn't say yes or no at first. He said: ask him why. The man said it describes the Most Merciful, and he loved to recite it. And the Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him. The approval is the teaching. The Prophet's silence, or his yes, to something done in front of him is reported too. Fourth, a fair note on who gathers them. Sunni scholars collect reports of the Prophet carried through his companions. Shia scholars also gather reports of the Prophet, and alongside them the sayings of the Imams of his family, weighed through their own collections and methods. Both treat a report about him as a serious thing to carry. So the next time a sentence starts with "the Prophet said", the question to hold is simple. Said, did, or approved? And who carried it here?
screen: `WHAT HE SAID.` · `WHAT HE DID.` · `WHAT HE APPROVED.` · `WHO GATHERS THE REPORTS.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one hadith. Take the one from today, slowly, in your own head: the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand others are safe. Let it sit. Now walk through your yesterday with it. Was there a moment your tongue wasn't safe for someone? A sharp text, a joke at someone's expense? Was there a moment your hands were a shelter instead, carrying, fixing, holding a door? Don't grade yourself. Just notice both. If you pray, you can ask for a safe tongue. If not, rest with the sentence until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Hadith. A report of what the Prophet said, did, or approved, carried by the people who saw and heard him. Today's word.
Your line: a report. Today, when you hear "the Prophet said", ask yourself: said, did, or approved? Tomorrow: sunnah and hadith. Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims read hadith in collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari, hear them quoted in Friday sermons and study circles, and Sunni and Shia scholars each gather and weigh reports through their own collections.

fork.setup: a man leading prayer ends his recitation with al-Ikhlas every time. people mention it to the Prophet. what does he do first?
options: tell them to ask the man why.
fork.reveal: he said: ask him why. the man loved that surah because it describes the Most Merciful, and the Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him.

original.note: a report, a piece of speech or news: in scholarship, a report about the Prophet.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hadith is a famous quote of the Prophet.
what it means: a report of what he said, did, or approved, carried by people who were there.
what a scholar hears: approval counts too: his yes, or his silence, to something done in front of him is reported and studied.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 676 (Aisha: he served his family, then went out to pray)
Sahih al-Bukhari 10 (the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe)
Sahih al-Bukhari 7375 (the man who recited al-Ikhlas in every prayer)

notes: Bukhari 676, 10 and 7375: confirm numbers and paraphrases. In 7375 the man recited al-Ikhlas at the end of each recitation in prayer; 'every time' is a simplification.
Definition of hadith as said, did, approved (qawl, fi'l, taqrir) follows the index line; some definitions add the Prophet's descriptions. Confirm wording.
Gloss of the Arabic 'hadith' as report, speech, news: confirm against a standard lexicon.
Shia description (reports of the Prophet and the sayings of the Imams, weighed through their own collections): confirm it is fair and framed without ranking.

Editor: the al-Ikhlas report now says he ended his recitation with it and that people 'mentioned it' (not 'complained'), in teach and fork, to match Bukhari 7375; the gloss of 'hadith' softened from an etymology to how it is usually translated.
